statement: In people who use ecstasy and are abstinent when scanned, binding of radioligands to the serotonin transporter is lower than in people who do not use it, in most but not all imaging studies. The figures here are second-hand, as summarized by a narrative review and a letter: in one study of 49 people who used ecstasy and 50 who did not, binding was lower throughout the cerebral cortex (-19% to -46%) and in the hippocampus (-21%), related to the extent of use and unchanged after control for the confounders the authors could address; in another, a group who preferred MDMA had lower binding in the neocortex (-56%), pallidostriatum (-19%) and amygdala (-32%), correlated with lifetime use, while a group who preferred hallucinogens showed none. In a prospective cohort with very low use, binding did not differ, although other imaging measures in that cohort did and its authors wrote that they could not exclude that even low doses are neurotoxic. A 2026 review summarizes a meta-analysis of 16 imaging studies in which binding was lower in 8 of 13 regions, with a positive association between binding and time abstinent that it says rested largely on one small study (Selvaraj et al., 2009), and a study of people abstinent about 2.5 years in which binding appeared to recover while verbal memory did not (Thomasius et al., 2006), a study that review had excluded from its own evidence base. What a lower binding signal means for nerve cells is disputed, and no primary imaging study was read for this claim. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Brain scans of people who use ecstasy often show less of a marker of serotonin nerve endings than scans of people who do not. The numbers here come from reviews, not from the scans themselves, and a lower signal does not by itself prove nerve cells were damaged.
population: Adults who use ecstasy recreationally, abstinent when scanned
exposure: Recreational ecstasy (MDMA) use, mostly moderate to heavy lifetime use
comparator: People who have not used ecstasy, or who use other drugs but not ecstasy
outcome: Serotonin transporter (SERT) binding measured with PET or SPECT
magnitude: Second-hand: -19% to -46% across cortical regions and -21% in the hippocampus (49 against 50 people, as summarized); -56% neocortex, -19% pallidostriatum, -32% amygdala in a group preferring MDMA, with no change in a group preferring hallucinogens. No intervals are given in the sources read; one prospective cohort of people with very low use (59 against 56) found no difference; and a meta-analysis of 16 imaging studies, summarized at second hand, reports lower binding in 8 of 13 regions and a possible recovery of binding with longer abstinence.

evidence.extracted: As summarized: 49 people with moderate ecstasy use against 50 people who did not use it; serotonin transporter binding lower in every region of the cerebral cortex (range -19% to -46%) and in the hippocampus (-21%), related to the extent of use (years, maximum dose); recent use confirmed by hair analysis, with other psychoactive drug use, sex, a gene polymorphism and chronic tolerance monitored; the review adds that studies of heavier use also found subcortical reductions (Kish et al., 2010).

evidence.extracted: As summarized: a group who preferred MDMA showed lower serotonin transporter binding potential in the neocortex (-56%), pallidostriatum (-19%) and amygdala (-32%), with the extent correlated with lifetime MDMA exposure, while a group who preferred hallucinogens (mainly LSD) showed no change (Erritzoe et al., 2011); a post-mortem case of one person who had used ecstasy as well as cocaine and heroin had striatal serotonin 60% to 77% below normal with normal dopamine (Kish et al., 2000).

risk_of_bias.note: Cross-sectional imaging comparisons with no pre-use scan, small samples and self-reported exposure, seen only through sources that do not appraise them.

inconsistency.note: The reviews themselves report that not every study found reductions, and a prospective cohort with very low use found none.

indirectness.note: Second-hand figures, and a binding signal is a surrogate: it can change without loss of nerve terminals.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the percentages are group differences in a surrogate marker between small selected samples (METHODS §6.3).

dose_response.note: Not applied: the dose relationships are reported second-hand and come from the same cross-sectional samples.

grade.reasoning: Observational imaging evidence starts low, downgraded for risk of bias (no pre-use scan, small selected samples), inconsistency (studies disagree, including a prospective cohort with no difference) and indirectness (second-hand, and the marker is a surrogate for terminal integrity). The claim is worded as an association in a measurement, not as damage.

verification.flag_note: Rests only on a narrative review, a letter and a correspondence; stays at draft (METHODS §6.3). The imaging studies themselves (Kish et al., 2010; Erritzoe et al., 2011; McCann et al., 2008; de Win et al., 2008) are not in this batch and should be read before this claim is shown.
